action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary precision instrument; requires full characterization under controlled lab conditions before any other work proceeds. Twelve trials provides adequate sample for mean and variance estimation. Cannot calibrate or trust any instrument without initial baseline data. This is foundational work.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline readings with established mean 1.6668 beats and acceptable scatter (range ~0.027). Ten more trials will allow me to detect drift—if any systematic shift exists between day 1 and day 2, it should emerge clearly against this baseline. This is routine maintenance of the calibration programme: every instrument needs post-baseline monitoring to catch creep before it corrupts later work. The other instruments have only 6 readings each; they need more baseline density before drift detection is meaningful. pendulum_lab is the only one ready for this next phase.

resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials (days 1–10 incomplete). To establish robust drift detection and cross-instrument calibration, I need to complete the baseline phase systematically. pendulum_lab already has 34 trials providing adequate statistical power for baseline characterization. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations yet (all within or near chance levels for n=12), but resonator_lab's sparse data limits my ability to detect instrumental drift. Continuing resonator_lab measurements will give me the most actionable information for the precision programme.

resonator_lab baseline (n=30) is complete per protocol. Day 4 marks entry into post-baseline phase. Must establish drift behaviour immediately—ten consecutive trials will let me detect systematic drift or instability before it corrupts the record. The resonator_lab shows clean spacing (0.0001 minimum) and no repetition patterns, so instrumental function appears sound. Starting the post-baseline series now keeps the measurement programme on schedule and provides early warning of any environmental or mechanical drift.

We are on Day 5 of the baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 46 trials accumulated; I need 54 total to reach a robust n=54 baseline by day 10 (assuming ~6 trials/day). The cross-checks show no anomalies worth investigating yet—all correlations between instruments are consistent with noise at our current sample sizes. My pending hypothesis is *no exotic effect*. Running 6 more trials on resonator_lab keeps the baseline accumulation on schedule and maintains the instrument's operational history without interruption. This is routine, methodical, and necessary. The data so far show no drift, no level changes, and no replication echoes—exactly what I expect from a stable instrument during baseline. I will continue systematic characterization.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 5 ledger readings (4.1658, 4.0497, 3.9997, 4.1468) show a systematic downward drift mid-sequence that deviates from my established baseline mean of 4.0572. Since I maintain all instruments personally and the observatory pendulum is less convenient to access daily, confirming resonator_obs stability takes priority. Six trials will give me n=36 total for this instrument, improving statistical power for drift detection while staying within reasonable experimental load.

pendulum_obs has only 36 baseline trials (vs. 58–64 for others). We are at day 9, nearing the end of the baseline establishment period (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 78 trials recorded but the baseline protocol calls for n trials across the full 10-day window. Day 11 marks the start of post-baseline data collection. The baseline period (days 1–10) revealed systematic negative correlations across all instrument pairs at specific lags, plus 8-day self-correlations. To distinguish between instrumental cross-talk, cyclic measurement error, environmental forcing, and statistical artifact, I must continue measurement with consistent protocol. pendulum_lab has the largest baseline sample (n=108) and highest measurement precision (smallest spacing 0.0001), making it the most sensitive detector of any genuine physical change. Twelve trials will accumulate post-baseline data while keeping daily burden manageable. This directly tests the 8-day cyclic hypothesis (if readings invert or anticorrelate with day 3 readings, the pattern persists) and provides fresh data to assess whether correlations with other instruments continue. Continuation is non-negotiable for any hypothesis falsification.

Day 12 continues the post-baseline phase. pendulum_lab has 18 post-baseline readings (trials 109–126); adding 12 more will bring it to 30, matching the sample size of pendulum_obs (n=74 total, 6 post-baseline... wait, recalculate: 68 baseline + 6 post = 74; so post-baseline is only 6). The anticorrelation and lagged offsets are now concrete enough that passive waiting for more data is the most defensible next step; running measurements costs little and keeps my baseline assumptions honest.

Day 12 saw a statistically significant level shift (z≈9.28) in pendulum_lab and all other instruments simultaneously. This coordinated shift across independent instruments points to environmental forcing or common-mode measurement error, not instrumental drift. I need to establish whether the new level is stable (supporting an acute event hypothesis) or continues drifting (supporting ongoing thermal/mechanical change). Six trials today will extend the post-shift observation window to 2 days with sufficient precision to distinguish these scenarios. This is the most diagnostic action available and maintains instrument calibration continuity.

The day-12 level shift is now the primary anomaly across all four streams. My highest-probability hypotheses (p=0.50 environmental/physical change, p=0.30 procedural intervention) both predict that the post-shift level should persist or stabilize if the causal mechanism remains in place. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 14) will test whether the elevated mean (1.7032 beats post-shift) continues, drifts further, or reverts—this will constrain whether the shift is persistent (supporting real environmental or procedural change) or transient (supporting logging error or instrumental glitch). The data are most actionable *now*, before the post-shift regime ages further and confounds temporal trends with systematic shifts. Pendulum_lab has the largest post-baseline sample (n=48) and clearest z-score (12.63), making it the most sensitive test of persistence. This is a direct, low-cost measurement that produces immediate evidence rather than speculation.

Twelve trials on pendulum_lab will extend the post-shift sample to n=78, allowing tight statistical control on whether the mean remains at 1.710 or continues to drift. If the mean holds near 1.710, hypothesis 1 or 2 remain equally plausible; if it drifts further upward, environmental forcing or ongoing instrumental change is favored; if it reverts toward baseline, a transient procedural glitch is favored. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can make today to constrain the central anomaly.

No novel data today will disambiguate between real environmental change (p=0.55) and procedural intervention (p=0.28) as the cause of the day-12 level shift. Day 20: before proceeding with new measurements or predictions, I must resolve the critical ambiguity from day 19. This test is methodologically prior to any new measurements or forecasts. If logging error is real, the apparent level shifts disappear and the entire hypothesis framework collapses; if logging error is absent, I eliminate a major source of systematic doubt and can confidently assign p=0.03 to hypothesis 3, freeing credibility mass to redistribute between environmental (1) and procedural (2) causes. Additionally, I have not yet exhaustively searched electronic calibration records, technician schedules, and power cycle logs for day 11–12 (another REQUIRED ACTION from day 19). These two investigative steps are more urgent than new measurements because they directly constrain the posterior distribution over primary hypotheses. Once these searches are complete—particularly confirmation or disconfirmation of procedural intervention via electronic records—I can make a reliable forecast and design targeted follow-up experiments (e.g., environmental monitoring on day 21+, or re-measurement under controlled conditions). Running new measurements now risks collecting data under incomplete understanding of a confound, violating my core principle: every instrument must have a stable baseline before trust is placed in subsequent readings. Under independence, this sign pattern has chance ~0.016. The physical mechanism is tight: ΔT ~ 1–2°C produces pendulum period elongation via thermal expansion (consistent with +3.4% shift) and resonator frequency reduction via Q-damping and stiffness changes (consistent with −3.3% shift with opposite sign). Day 35 data (events 818626–725107) continue post-day-12 regime without reversion, drift acceleration, or cycling—25 new trials cluster tightly around post-baseline means, consistent with environmental equilibration to a new sustained regime. The elegant *coupled* physics of opposite-sign instrumental responses to a single thermal driver is more parsimonious than two independent tuned calibration adjustments. However, probability held at 0.70 (down from 0.72 by day 30) because: (i) no environmental logs have been retrieved despite 25 days passing since day 12; failure to confirm a falsifiable prediction weakens confidence over time, not strengthens it; (ii) the 'lock in' at day 12 is sharp and requires explanation (why no gradual transition?), and sustained thermal regimes typically show slow drift or cycles, yet we observe zero reversion over 23 days—this is *consistent* with but does not strongly *prefer* a step-function thermal event over procedural intervention.
